title: Hiring is Obsolete: why young hackers should start startups instead of taking jobs
summary: Paul Graham argues that falling startup costs shift power from employers and investors to young hackers. Rather than being undervalued as employees, talented people can be valued directly by users and acquirers by building something people want. Big companies will increasingly buy early startups, fusing recruiting and product development.

principles.text: Cheaper startups reduce investors' power over founders, since their leverage comes from money.
principles.quote: Investors' power comes from money. When startups need less money, investors have less power over them.

principles.text: A startup's goal is to make something users want, not write cool software; look at users.
principles.quote: The goal in a startup is not to write a cool piece of software. It's to make something people want. And to do that you have to look at users-- forget about hacking, and just look at users.

principles.text: Successful startups solve a specific problem people already know they have.
principles.quote: Most successful startups not only do something very specific, but solve a problem people already know they have.

principles.text: Online, good products spread by word of mouth, so marketing spend matters less.
principles.quote: On the Internet, anything genuinely good will spread by word of mouth.

principles.text: Selling directly teaches developers more than focus groups do.
principles.quote: It's painful doing sales, but you learn much more from trying to sell people something than reading what they said in focus groups.

principles.text: Take big risks while young: risk and reward are proportionate, and most people avoid extreme choices, which reduces competition.
principles.quote: Extreme choices like starting a startup are so frightening that most people won't even try. So you don't end up having as much competition as you might expect, considering the prizes at stake.
